title: Robinhood Alternatives for Beginner Investors (2026)
body_markdown:
> The best Robinhood alternatives for beginners in 2026 are Bloom, Fidelity Youth Account, Schwab Teen Investor Account, Acorns, and Greenlight. Bloom stands out for teens aged 13+ and young adults who want real stocks, crypto, structured lessons, and an AI investing assistant in one app. Robinhood requires users to be 18+ to actively use the platform themselves — and while it does offer a UTMA custodial account, that account is adult-controlled and gifting-oriented, not a hands-on experience the teen operates directly.


If you've opened Robinhood, looked around, and felt like it wasn't built for someone just starting out — you're not wrong. The platform assumes you already know what you're doing. There's no guided curriculum, no AI to answer basic questions, and if you're under 18, you can't use it yourself at all. Finding a real Robinhood alternative for beginners takes some digging. This guide does that work for you.


Below is a fair breakdown of five alternatives, a side-by-side comparison table, and two clear pathways: one for parents researching custodial accounts for a teenager, and one for young adults aged 18 to 24 who want stocks, crypto, and education in a single app.


*Pricing and features are current as of September 2026. Details change frequently — verify directly with each provider before signing up.*


### The 5 Best Robinhood Alternatives for Beginners


#### Bloom


[Bloom](https://bloomapp.com/) is built specifically for people who are new to investing — whether that's a 15-year-old learning with a parent's help or a 22-year-old opening their first brokerage account.


Inside the app, you can trade real fractional stocks, ETFs, and crypto. This isn't a simulator. Your money is in real markets, with SIPC coverage up to $500,000.


What separates Bloom from everything else on this list is the learning layer. There are more than 300 lesson modules covering topics from what a stock actually is to how to read a balance sheet. Lessons are short and quiz-based, so you build real knowledge without sitting through hour-long videos. When you get stuck, Bloomie — the built-in AI assistant — answers your questions in plain language.


Beyond the basics, Bloom lets you mirror the portfolios of well-known Wall Street investors and politicians, build theme-based portfolios around ideas you actually care about, and compete in investing tournaments to earn in-app rewards called Oinks. That combination of real investing, structured education, and competitive engagement doesn't exist anywhere else at this price point.


For families, Bloom offers custodial teen accounts for users aged 13 and up. The teen actively uses the app themselves — a meaningful difference from platforms where a parent controls everything and the child is essentially a passive beneficiary.


**Pricing:** $15 per month or $69.99 per year for individual accounts. Custodial accounts are $150 per year ($150 per year includes all children in the household).


#### Fidelity Youth Account


Fidelity's Youth Account is a strong free option for teenagers. It's teen-owned rather than custodial — the minor holds the account in their own name, with a parent or guardian linked. No subscription fee, no trading commissions, no minimum balance.


The catch: a parent must already have a Fidelity brokerage account to open one. If your family doesn't use Fidelity, there's a setup step before your teen can do anything.


Fidelity Youth doesn't offer gamification, an AI assistant, or portfolio mirroring. The educational content is lighter than what Bloom provides. For a teen who wants to learn investing as a skill — not just hold a few shares — that gap matters.


#### Schwab Teen Investor Account


Charles Schwab launched its Teen Investor Account in March 2026. It's a joint brokerage account for users aged 13 to 17, with zero commissions and no subscription fee. Schwab's reputation for reliability and customer service is a genuine plus.


Like Fidelity Youth, it doesn't offer gamification, AI guidance, or mirroring features. NerdWallet has described it as less compelling for mobile-first traders who want an engaging, interactive experience. If your teenager learns better through an app than a traditional brokerage interface, that's worth factoring in.


#### Acorns


Acorns takes a completely different approach. Rather than picking stocks, you connect a debit or credit card and Acorns rounds up your purchases to the nearest dollar, automatically investing the spare change into pre-built ETF portfolios.


That hands-off model works well for people who struggle to save consistently. But it's not a platform for learning how to invest. You can't buy individual stocks, you can't trade crypto, and there are no teen-specific features. Pricing runs approximately $3 to $12 per month depending on the plan, as of September 2026.


If your goal is to build investing knowledge alongside a real portfolio, Acorns isn't designed for that.


#### Greenlight


Greenlight is primarily a debit card and family finance app — chores, allowances, spending controls — with investing added as a secondary feature. Plans run from approximately $5.99 to $19.98 per month per family, as of September 2026.


The investing component lets kids buy fractional shares of stocks and ETFs, with parental approval required on each trade. There's no crypto trading, no AI assistant, and no structured curriculum comparable to Bloom's 300+ modules.


Greenlight is a reasonable choice if you want one app to manage a child's debit card and pocket money with some investing on the side. It's not the right fit if investing education is the main goal.

### Which Path Is Right for You?


#### Parents and Teens Aged 13 to 17


If you're a parent looking for a custodial investing account your teenager will actually use, the key question is whether you want passive or active learning.


Fidelity Youth and Schwab Teen are both solid free options from established institutions. They're appropriate if your goal is simply to open an account and let your teen hold a few positions. Neither will teach your teen how markets work in any structured way.


Bloom's custodial account is designed for teens who want to learn. Your teenager logs in, completes lessons, asks Bloomie questions, mirrors a portfolio they find interesting, and trades fractional shares of real assets. The $150 per year fee reflects that depth. For families where financial education is the point — not just account access — Bloom is the stronger option.


Robinhood does offer a UTMA custodial account, but it's adult-controlled and oriented around gifting assets to a minor. The teen doesn't operate it themselves, which makes it a fundamentally different product from Bloom's teen account or Fidelity Youth.


#### Young Adults Aged 18 to 24


Once you turn 18, teen-specific accounts are no longer relevant. You can open a standard Robinhood account — but if you're reading this, you already know Robinhood isn't built for learning.


For self-directed beginners who want stocks, ETFs, and crypto alongside real education, Bloom's individual plan is worth a serious look. The 300+ lesson modules give you a curriculum to work through at your own pace. Bloomie answers questions without judgment. The tournament and mirroring features make the early months of investing more engaging than watching a portfolio that barely moves.


Acorns is an option if you want automation over engagement. Greenlight isn't built for adults. Fidelity and Schwab have strong full-service platforms, but neither is designed to walk you through the fundamentals the way Bloom is.


If you're 18 to 24, new to investing, and want one app that handles education and real trading together, Bloom is the clearest fit among the alternatives here.


### Get Started


Ready to try the alternative built for beginners? Visit[bloomapp.com](https://bloomapp.com/) to get started with Bloom today.


### Frequently Asked Questions


**What is the best Robinhood alternative for teenagers?** Bloom is the strongest option for teenagers who want to actively learn and invest. It offers custodial accounts for users aged 13 and up, more than 300 lesson modules, an AI assistant called Bloomie, and real fractional stock, ETF, and crypto trading. Fidelity Youth and Schwab Teen Investor are solid free alternatives from established brokerages, though neither offers structured education, AI guidance, or gamification.


**Can a 15-year-old use Robinhood?** No. Robinhood requires users to be 18 or older to actively use the platform themselves. Robinhood does offer a UTMA custodial account, but it's controlled by an adult and oriented around gifting assets to a minor — not an account the teenager operates directly. For a 15-year-old who wants to invest and learn hands-on, Bloom's custodial teen account or the Fidelity Youth Account are better fits.


**Is there a free alternative to Robinhood for teens?** Yes. The Fidelity Youth Account and the Schwab Teen Investor Account (launched March 2026) are both free, with no subscription fees and no trading commissions. Both require a parent to have an existing account with the same institution. Neither offers gamification, AI assistance, or a structured investing curriculum, so they're better suited to teens who want basic account access rather than guided learning.


**Does Bloom offer crypto trading?** Yes. Bloom lets users trade cryptocurrency alongside real fractional stocks and ETFs within the same app. It's one of the few beginner-focused investing platforms that combines crypto access with structured financial education and an AI assistant.


**How does Bloom compare to Acorns for a beginner?** Acorns automates saving by rounding up purchases and investing spare change into pre-built ETF portfolios — useful if you want a hands-off approach, but it doesn't offer individual stock or crypto trading, and there's no educational curriculum or teen-specific features. Bloom is the better choice for beginners who want to understand what they're investing in and build real knowledge alongside a real portfolio.


*Disclosure: Pricing and product features change frequently. All details in this article are current as of September 2026. Readers should verify current pricing, account eligibility, and features directly with each provider before making any investment decisions.*
